svg.title: Inside one reply
svg.desc: One reply of a language model, step by step: reading the window, thinking, answering and stopping, with panels on effort, thinking, token sampling, output limits, time and price.
svg.text: What happens between sending the window and getting an answer: how each token is picked, what thinking is, and what sets the wait and the price.
Panels A to E show parts of it in more detail. The numbers are for one example reply.
The model gets the whole window, and processes only the part that is not cached.
48,000 tokens read for the last request: cached
2,000 new tokens: the latest tool result
Without the cache, all 50,000 tokens would be processed again on every request. [3] Most harnesses send the whole window each time, and
some providers can keep it on their servers. [4, 5]
The model writes text for itself, one token at a time.
users are logged out after a minute, so check the timeout units ...
You wait here: the thinking is written before any answer appears.
It writes the reply or a tool call, one token at a time.
500 answer tokens, shown to you as they are written
Thinking and answer together count toward the output limit.
The reply ends in one of three ways.
End of answer: the harness shows the
Tool call: the harness runs it, adds the
result and sends a new request.
Output limit reached: the reply is cut off
After a tool call, the whole window is read again, and only the new part is processed.
cached: read for the last request
new: the tool call and its result
In an agent this repeats for every tool call, often dozens of times in one task.
Times are illustrative and prices are made up. Thinking is the biggest part of this bill: the 3,000 thinking tokens cost three times as much as the
Model: the neural network that reads text and images and writes
text, for example Claude Opus, GPT or Gemini. Open-weight
models such as Qwen or DeepSeek can also run on your own
Harness: the program around the model. It builds the context
window, sends it to the model, runs the tools and asks for your
permission. For example Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI,
Provider: the company that runs the model on its servers, for
example Anthropic, OpenAI or Google. It bills per token, or per
month with limits counted in tokens.
Token: a word or a piece of a word. 1,000 tokens are roughly 550
to 750 English words, depending on the model. [1, 2]
Request: one round trip. The model gets the whole context
Context window: all the text the model reads to write its next
reply. Its size has a limit, for example 1,000,000 tokens.
Cache: the provider's store of work already done on the start of a
window. It is kept for a few minutes, and a request that starts with
Effort, or thinking level, is a setting that the harness sends with
each request. The names differ between providers, for example
none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh or max. [4, 5, 6]
Higher effort makes the model think longer and check more,
often with more tool calls, and it changes the answer too. That
costs time and tokens. It often helps on hard tasks, and on easy
ones it wastes time and tokens. [4, 6]
Effort is guidance, and the amount of thinking still varies from
Each token is picked by chance
After "The tests", the next token could be:
At each step the model gives every possible next token a
probability. The provider then picks one at random, weighted by
Temperature sets how often the pick goes past the most likely
token. Some models let the harness set it, and on others it is
Two runs with the same window:
Each picked token becomes part of the text for the next step, so
one different pick can change the rest of the reply.
Users are logged out after exactly one minute. Maybe
the timeout is stored in seconds but compared in
The timeout was in seconds, not milliseconds. I changed
Before it answers, the model can write text for itself: it plans,
tries ideas and checks them. The answer can then use what the
Thinking tokens are billed as output, count toward the output
limit, and take space in the window. [4, 5, 7]
What OpenAI, Google and Anthropic show you: [4, 5, 7]
Whether the next request still contains the thinking depends on
the model: some keep it, some drop it. [4, 7]
Two limits: the window and the reply
this reply, up to the output limit
Output limit for one reply, for example 128,000 tokens [8]
The window limit covers everything in one request: what the
model reads and what it writes. The output limit is smaller and
covers one reply, thinking and answer together. [8]
When a reply reaches the output limit, it stops in the middle.
Long thinking can use up the whole limit before any answer
Input and reply share the window, so a nearly full window leaves
What sets the wait and the price
Reading is fast because the model processes all the new input at
once. Writing is slow because each token takes its own step. So
you wait mostly for thinking and long answers.
Price for the example reply, in cents
Made-up prices per million tokens, in the range of real ones: input $1.50, cached
Providers charge per token. Output costs several times more
than input, and cached input a fraction of input. [2, 3] Thinking is
Writing to the cache can cost a little extra the first time, for
example 1.25 times the input price at Anthropic. [3]
An agent sends the whole window again for every tool call, so
over a session the cache cuts most of the cost of reading it. [3]

Sources, read in November 2026: [1] OpenAI, "Key concepts", tokens (developers.openai.com/api/docs/concepts); [2] Anthropic, "Pricing" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing); [3] Anthropic, "Prompt caching" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching); [4] OpenAI, "Reasoning models"

(developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning); [5] Google, "Gemini thinking" (ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/thinking); [6] Anthropic, "Effort" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort); [7] Anthropic, "Thinking" (platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/thinking); [8] Anthropic, "Context windows"
(platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows). Token counts, times and probabilities are illustrative, and prices are made up.
